reasons: [alternatives_counterarguments/major] D1 [verdict para 1 and 3; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion item 1; edgeCasesAndFailureModes last item; alternatives (no status-quo option); K8] The draft never compares either route with the status quo of no new channel, where we keep the EUR 0.8M/yr existing direct base at full margin with no added cost. It also never states the absolute break-evens that its own model implies. Using the draft's formulas: Meridian's contribution is S*(g-0.35), so every channel sale loses money if gross margin g is 35% or less. Direct at plan is 7.0g - 3.1, which is negative unless g > 44.3%. If finance's 7.0M includes the 2.4M base, the incremental revenue is only 4.6M, and the team needs g > ~67% to beat doing nothing. The draft says 'below about 22% would favour direct even at Meridian's face value' (furtherResearch, edgeCases). That is misleading: at g < 22% both routes have negative contribution and neither should be chosen. The verdict's fallback ('build the direct DE/NL team') could therefore destroy value. The draft gives no margin threshold below which that fallback is wrong.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [verdict para 1 last sentence; practicalImplications last item; counterarguments item 3] The decision rule in the verdict does not follow from the draft's own economics. The draft finds that Meridian at the 60% reference delivery rate beats direct at any margin when the base is treated consistently (CL3, K17). Direct wins only in the cannibalisation scenario at g > ~26% (K9). Yet the verdict says that if Meridian refuses minimums, we should 'build the direct DE/NL team'. A refusal does not change the expected-value comparison. At most it raises downside variance, which the draft does not quantify. The rule also never asks whether an existing-account carve-out alone, without minimums, would keep Meridian ahead (K9 says it would).

[decision_usefulness/major] D3 [CL15; K11-K13; practicalImplications item 3; counterarguments item 3; verdict para 1] The minimum-purchase test is rigged. Minimums are set at 100% of Meridian's projected net purchases (EUR 1.63M/2.6M/3.58M, K11-K13), measured excluding carved-out accounts. If Meridian's 12M includes the existing base (unknown, G2), this asks for more than Meridian's own number. The only quantitative reference shows 60% delivery, and a credible distributor would normally reject 100%-of-forecast minimums. Typical practice ties minimums to a share of forecast, and E9 cites shortfall-percentage triggers. So the conclusion that 'a refusal is itself information that the projection is not credible' does not hold. The draft should propose a minimum level, or a floor below which the deal is uneconomic, using the delivery-rate and margin break-evens. It should not anchor to the headline figure.

[coverage/major] D4 [practicalImplications item 3; verdict para 1; C4 assessment] The request asks 'on what terms', and the packet names the discount level as a lever. The draft only says 'Review of the discount level' and gives no target. Discount is the largest economic lever in its own model: each 5 points on 7.2M of sell-through is about EUR 0.36M, comparable to the EUR 0.58M margin-independent gap (K17). The draft could have used E11 (35% is at or above typical distributor gross margins) and a break-even to propose a range, or a lower discount on legacy accounts. The renewal terms are equally vague ('no auto-renewal, or short notice', with no notice period proposed).

[reasoning_validity/major] D5 [CL3; CL9 (material flag); K17; C1 assessment bullet 2] CL3 states 'Meridian stays ahead at any margin' at 60% delivery. That rests on a EUR 0.58M cost gap (K17). It ignores Meridian-side internal costs: channel manager, FAE or pre-sales support, training, MDF and RMA (E12). These can plausibly match or exceed EUR 0.58M over 3 years, and the 'zero headcount' correction itself says they are not zero. The draft says these costs and direct's uncosted logistics 'push in opposite directions', but CL3 is still stated unconditionally. CL9 ('zero headcount' is wrong) is marked material:false, although it directly decides whether the K17 advantage survives. The draft should state the conclusion conditionally, or give a support-cost break-even.

[coverage/major] D6 [C1 and C6 assessments; tradeoffs] The decision objective covers 3-year 'and post-term' contribution. The draft does not analyse post-term economics. Under direct, the cost is front-loaded during ramp, and by Y3 we would have a ramped team and owned accounts. The Meridian route faces the month-24 notice deadline, the auto-renewal to month 60, and possible indemnity on exit. The draft treats C6 only qualitatively, and it never asks whether direct's 3-year loss or low return is an investment that pays back in Y4-Y5. A 3-year comparison structurally penalises the route with fixed ramp costs.
D5 remedy both (Meridian-side internal support cost benchmark); D1-D4, D6 reanalysis

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [CL15; C4 assessment (a) first sub-bullet; C4 mechanisms ('cap our downside at the level where Meridian still beats direct'); verdict 'Terms to ask for' item 3; K31, K32, K36] The draft says the proposed 60% minimums 'sit above the illustrative 49-53% break-even delivery rate against direct' and that they 'cap our downside at the level where Meridian still beats direct'. K31 and K32 only support this when both figures exclude the base. The draft applies the same reasoning to its EUR 3.74M variant, where Meridian's EUR 12M includes the carved-out base and only EUR 9.6M is incremental. Recomputing with the draft's own formula, 9.6d(g-0.35) - 0.48 = 7g - 3.1, gives a break-even delivery rate of about 61% at g = 50% (0.88/1.44) and about 66% at g = 60% (1.58/2.40). In that case a 60% minimum is below break-even, so Meridian trails direct even when it meets the minimum. This matches the draft's own K41 (direct leads above 48.7% at 60% delivery), so the minimum-setting logic contradicts the draft's own break-even analysis. The draft should give scenario-specific break-evens, or set minimums above break-even in the base-included case (about 61-66%, or the K36 equivalent).

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [verdict para 2 (third bullet); CL16; alternatives 'Status quo'; practicalImplications item 1 and last item; furtherResearch item 1] Carried forward from prior D6 (partially fixed). Post-term economics are now covered illustratively (K38-K40), but the decision rule ignores them. The verdict and CL16 say flatly that 'below roughly 42%, neither route should be chosen' and that direct needs g > 44.3% (K19), or 67.4% (K20), to beat the status quo. These are 3-year floors. The draft's own C6 mechanism says that 'fixed ramp costs make a 3-year comparison structurally unfavourable to direct, because the payback falls in Y4+'. A direct team that loses money over 3 years at g = 40% could still be value-creating over 5 years. The status quo also forgoes EU growth and capability (C5, C6), and the rule ignores this. The floors should be labelled 3-year floors, and the 'neither route' rule should depend on finance's Y4+ run-rate.

[decision_usefulness/major] D3 [verdict para 3 ('the preferred route is Meridian on revised terms'); alternatives 'Meridian on revised terms'; K24, K25, K30; C6] The verdict names 'Meridian on revised terms' as the preferred route, yet its own figures put the two routes close to a tie. In the base-excluded carve-out case, Meridian's lead after one channel manager and one FAE is 0.10 + 0.2g: about EUR 0.20M at g = 50% over 3 years (K30). MDF of EUR 0.09-0.23M is computed on net purchases (K24, K25). E19 says 'partner-sourced revenue', and on the EUR 7.2M sell-through base MDF would be EUR 0.14-0.36M, which wipes out the lead. The draft itself says K23 is 'likely understated': it leaves out bonus (E15: EUR 12-42k), car, travel and NL staff. In the base-included case direct leads above 48.7% (K41). C6 (owned relationships, post-term run-rate) points towards direct. The verdict's own text ('Meridian is not clearly better on 3-year economics') contradicts naming Meridian as preferred. What actually tips the deal towards Meridian is the 25-30% discount ask (EUR 0.36-0.72M, K37), but the preference is not made conditional on it. The verdict should present this as a near-tie that depends on (a) the carve-out, (b) a discount reduction and (c) a lean support plan. It should also explain why C6 and post-term value do not reverse the ranking.
